title: Nund Rishi Plants Kashmir's Ethic
subtitle: How a Kashmiri Saint Turned Labor and Restraint into a Valley’s Quiet Law
region: Kulgam, Charar-e-Sharif and the Kashmir Valley
moral: Shared ethics can outlive arguments over labels.

sources.citation: Nund Rishi's Shruks in Kashmiri oral and manuscript tradition
sources.note: Primary verse tradition, without autograph manuscripts.

sources.citation: Khwaja Azam Diddamari, Tarikh-i-Azami, 1736, and Rishi Namah traditions
sources.note: Later Persian and hagiographic sources for the Rishi order.

sources.citation: Mohammad Ishaq Khan, Kashmir's Transition to Islam (1994); Mridu Rai, Hindu Rulers, Muslim Subjects (2004); Triloki Nath Raina, An Introduction to Kashmiri Language and Literature (1972)
sources.note: Modern work on Rishi Sufism and Kashmiri language history.

panels.shot: wide, misty valley vista with low-angle focus on Nund Rishi seated under a tall chinar, mountains looming behind

dialogue.text: In a Kashmir of temples, shrines and rival claims, Nund Rishi spoke in Kashmiri of labor, restraint and mercy—and his quiet ethic outlived the arguments over who owned the valley’s soul.

panels.shot: slow push-in from high valley view towards a modest village near Kulgam

dialogue.text: Late fourteenth-century Kashmir was a valley between worlds—old Shaiva and Buddhist lineages, new sultans and Sufis, villagers watching from their fields and hearths.

panels.shot: medium shot of the young Nund Rishi in a village lane, half in shadow, half in light

dialogue.text: Out of Kulgam’s earth came Noor-ud-Din, later called Nund Rishi—a village boy watching sharp tongues and soft hearts share the same streets.

panels.shot: interior wide of a simple wooden room where elders debate, Nund Rishi listens at the edge

dialogue.text: New Muslim sultans ruled from Srinagar, land grants shifted, shrines jostled for favor. Villagers weighed fear and hope, and the words for God changed on official tongues.

panels.shot: soft wide shot by a riverbank with Lal Ded as a distant, anonymous figure; Nund Rishi watches in awe

dialogue.text: Tradition remembers him hearing Lal Ded’s Kashmiri verses on the road and riverbank—an older voice tearing at empty ritual, praising inner truth in the valley’s own tongue.

panels.shot: close-up on Nund Rishi’s face as he hears verses, eyes reflecting water and firelight

dialogue.text: Her shivras spoke of the divine beyond label, mocked hypocrisy. For a young Noor-ud-Din, they showed that the valley’s everyday speech could carry the weight of awakening.

panels.shot: wide shot of a hillside cave or hut where Nund Rishi sits alone in meditation

dialogue.text: He turned inward, took the path of a Muslim faqir, but not of imported Persian orders. In his solitude the shape of an indigenous Kashmiri Rishi way began to form.

panels.shot: medium shot in a simple orchard where Nund Rishi works with his hands, villagers watch

dialogue.text: He refused luxury, worked the earth with his own hands. His path made labor itself a devotion—and shamed holy men who lived off gifts while preaching renunciation.

panels.shot: intimate interior shot of a hut with Nund Rishi dictating shruks to a disciple by lamplight

dialogue.text: His shruks—short Kashmiri verses—poured out of this hut and field, praising restraint, mercy and simple living. In them, the valley’s speech became a language of Sufi reflection.

panels.shot: close-up of Nund Rishi’s hand scattering grain to birds outside, disciples watch

dialogue.text: Khwaja Azam Diddamari later wrote of his tenderness—feeding birds, refusing violence. The Rishi ethic held that harming creatures darkened the heart and the valley together.

panels.shot: medium shot of Nund Rishi speaking to a mixed group near Charar-e-Sharif, shrine and village in background

dialogue.text: “If you till, eat, and share with restraint, the quarrel over names loses its sting.”

panels.shot: wide crowd shot, some in Hindu dress, some in Muslim, listening under tall trees

dialogue.text: His circle drew Hindus and Muslims. He did not erase difference; he planted a shared ethic—honest work, self-restraint, compassion—as the ground they could stand on together.

panels.shot: documentary-style montage wide: Sufi khanqah, temple, and Rishi hut all in one valley frame

dialogue.text: Modern historians see the Rishi order as one stream in Kashmir’s gradual Islamization—alongside court politics, land disputes, and other Sufi networks, not as the single tide that turned the valley.

panels.shot: medium shot of Nund Rishi gently declining rich gifts from a courtier, villagers watch

dialogue.text: Stories in Rishi Namah remember him turning away from sultans’ favors, wary of courts that mixed piety with power and used religion to sanctify new hierarchies.

panels.shot: low-angle shot of Nund Rishi under a tree, quoting Lal Ded, mountains behind

dialogue.text: He praised Lal Ded’s wisdom in his shruks, naming a woman saint from an older Shaiva world as a teacher. In that gesture, he stitched traditions without erasing their edges.

panels.shot: interior hut shot with Nund Rishi frail in final days, disciples around in silence

dialogue.text: He died around 1438, in a Kashmir still full of tension and difference. His passing did not end conflict—but it left an order whose measure of holiness was humility and service.

panels.shot: wide shot of Charar-e-Sharif shrine through time: subtle visual cues of changing architecture and pilgrims

dialogue.text: Charar-e-Sharif became the heart of the Rishi memory, rebuilt and revisited across centuries—its wooden beams holding stories of famine, fire, and still, people gathering for Nund Rishi’s verses.

panels.shot: close-up of an old Kashmiri manuscript of shruks, pages gently turned by unseen hands

dialogue.text: Without an autograph, his shruks live in oral chains, manuscripts, and memory. Through them, Kashmiri itself survived as a language that could speak of God, ethics and doubt.

panels.shot: final sweeping wide of Kashmir valley at dawn, faint overlay of Nund Rishi’s figure seated under a chinar

dialogue.text: In a land still marked by contesting labels, Nund Rishi endures as a reminder that a shared ethic—work, restraint, mercy—can be the valley’s true shrine, if people choose to inhabit it.
